titleStmt.title: Tonotopic Organization in the Depth of Human Inferior Colliculus
titleStmt.author: Ress
Chandrasekaran

bibl.title: Tonotopic Organization in the Depth of Human Inferior Colliculus

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: frequency representation across the depth of the human inferior colliculus
span.quote: The goal of this study is to examine frequency representation in the human IC using high-resolution (1.2 mm) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 3 T, adapted for auditory stimulation.

span.label: whether tonotopic gradients in human IC can be measured at all at conventional 3 T field strength
span.quote: While these studies demonstrate the utility of very high-field strengths in resolving tonotopic gradients within the IC, it is unclear whether clear tonotopy is evident at smaller field strengths.

span.label: shows laminar tonotopy in human IC at 3 T using 1.2 mm imaging and virtual depth penetrations, and finds it patchy rather than continuous
span.quote: The results confirm a laminar tonotopy in the human IC at 3 T, but with a heterogeneous, patchy character.

span.label: existence
span.quote: Results show statistically significant tonotopic gradients within both ICs of all subjects.

span.label: tonotopy in the inferior colliculus
span.quote: The goal of this study is to examine frequency representation in the human IC using high-resolution (1.2 mm) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 3 T, adapted for auditory stimulation.

span.label: fmri
span.quote: Imaging was performed on a 3 T scanner (GE Signa Excite HD) using an eight-channel head coil.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Because BOLD reports synaptic input and local-circuit activity more than output spiking, the measured map tracks the interdigitated tonotopy of cochlear-nucleus afferents rather than the smooth map of IC neurons, producing patches.
span.quote: Accordingly, our results may more closely reflect the patchy, somewhat interdigitated tonotopic organization of bottom-up neuronal inputs to IC from the cochlear nucleus, as reported by anterograde labeling studies (Oliver and Morest, 1984 ; Hofstetter and Ehret, 1992 ; Loftus et al., 2008 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: At 3 T half the BOLD signal is intravascular, so tissue near large draining veins yields strong contrast and tissue away from them yields little, imposing a vascular patch pattern on the frequency map.
span.quote: If so, the observed patchy structure may reflect stronger contrast from regions of IC where there are larger concentrations of draining veins, while little contrast is observed in other regions.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Attentive auditory tasks bias processing to the left hemisphere, and largely ipsilateral corticocollicular feedback carries that bias down to the colliculus, yielding stronger left-IC gradients.
span.quote: Auditory tasks that require attentive processing are known to show a left-hemispheric bias (Bryden et al., 1983 ) and can modulate IC activity via corticocollicular connections (Rinne et al., 2007 , 2008 ).

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Each voxel averages millions of neurons of mixed frequency preference, so within-voxel heterogeneity broadens the apparent tuning and compresses the measured gradient range.
span.quote: Each voxel encompasses a volume of ∼1.7 μL containing several million neurons, so some heterogeneity of response can be expected.

span.label: a surface model of the IC allows virtual penetrations normal to the tissue, a hemodynamic analogue of an electrode track
span.quote: Thus, the notion of using tissue depth as a reference frame was proven to work fairly well, despite the patchy character of the data.

span.label: sparse sampling puts the acquisition in the flat top of the BOLD response and in a quiet gap, so scanner noise does not drive the measurement
span.quote: In sparse-sampling designs, one attempts to sample the hyperoxic peak of the BOLD response evoked by preceding stimulus, then allocate a sufficient delay to allow that response to decay away before the next sample is obtained. Moreover, the delay is adjusted so that the nuisance response from the scanner-acquisition noise is minimized

span.label: three-shot spiral acquisition acts as a temporal anti-aliasing filter against cardiac and respiratory noise, avoiding the need for gating
span.quote: The use of the three-shot spiral acquisition acts as a temporal anti-aliasing filter that substantially reduces high-frequency physiological nuisance effects, particularly cardiac pulsations. In single-shot acquisition, each fMRI slice is acquired very quickly (∼20–30 ms) compared to hemodynamic time scales, but the samples are widely spaced (e.g., 2–3 s). This results in aliasing of high-frequency fluctuations driven by cardiac pulse (>1 Hz) and respiration (∼0.25 Hz). In our multi-shot imaging, acquisition is now distributed over multiple brief sampling periods separated by the relatively short TR = 1 s. This preparation implements a low-pass filter upon the data.

span.label: the external cortex is identified and discarded before the depth analysis because tonotopy is not a feature of it
span.quote: Since tonotopy is not a feature of the external cortex of the IC, this region is ignored in the subsequent depth analysis.

span.label: an adaptive staircase on a frequency-discrimination task holds attention roughly constant throughout scanning
span.quote: During stimulus periods, the frequency difference, typically 3–8%, between the two sounds was adjusted in real time using a pair of randomly interleaved two-up, one-down staircases. After each run, the subject’s current frequency-discrimination threshold value was estimated as the average frequency difference over the latter half of the trials in that run. Frequency difference for the next run was then initialized to a value 30% greater than this estimate. This creates a stable pattern of performance in which subjects perform very well on the task at the start of each run, and then steadily return to their threshold value

span.label: Curvature causes deep voxels to be resampled by adjacent virtual penetrations.
span.quote: Another drawback of the depth-penetration approach is that voxels in deeper regions tend to get more heavily resampled by adjacent penetrations because of curvature effects.

span.label: The high-resolution acquisition had low thermal SNR (~20-30 versus >100 in conventional fMRI).
span.quote: Our high-resolution data had comparatively high levels of thermal noise.

span.label: Voxel-level frequency tuning was broad rather than narrow, most likely because of the spatial resolution.
span.quote: We did not observe narrow frequency tuning in our voxels, particularly at intermediate frequencies.

span.label: The measured depth gradients covered only part of the 5-octave stimulus range.
span.quote: Also, the observed depth gradients did not span the full range of the stimuli.

span.label: The patchiness and between-subject variability limit the method's usefulness for planning midbrain implant placement.
span.quote: While our data demonstrates tonotopic representation as a function of depth, we find that tonotopic gradients are patchy and variable across individuals, which could pose a significant challenge for the placement of midbrain implants.

span.label: only 18% of the total bilateral IC area showed significant depth gradients
span.quote: Areas of significant depth gradients varied from 19 to 32 mm 2 (mean across subjects of 25 mm 2 ), which was 18% of the total area of bilateral IC.

span.label: the mean gradient is about half what would be needed to span the stimulus range across the tissue depth
span.quote: Mean gradient was 0.53 octaves/mm, about half of what would be required to linearly resolve the full stimulus gamut in a 5-mm depth of tissue (see Discussion ).

span.label: reversed gradients appear at the margins, attributed to the curvature of the structure
span.quote: However, IC has a great deal more curvature than SC, so it is not surprising that we see some regions of reverse gradients at the margins of the colliculi, particularly on caudal regions where curvature is largest.

span.label: deep voxels are resampled by adjacent penetrations because of curvature
span.quote: Another drawback of the depth-penetration approach is that voxels in deeper regions tend to get more heavily resampled by adjacent penetrations because of curvature effects.

span.label: the patchiness could be neural, from task-related recruitment, or hemodynamic - the paper offers both and settles neither
span.quote: On the neural side, the observed patchiness could be the consequence of task-related recruitment of sub-regions of IC tissue. Task demands such as selective attention have been shown to affect IC (Rinne et al., 2008 ), but such effects have not yet been evaluated at these fine spatial scales.

span.label: four male subjects
span.quote: Subjects were four male adults (age range 21–31), with normal hearing (air-conduction thresholds <20 dB nHL for octaves from 0.25 to 8 kHz).

span.label: gradients were markedly stronger on the left colliculus than the right, without an account
span.quote: Gradients were typically stronger and more extensive on the left colliculus then on the right. Left-colliculus gradients were typically larger on the lateral and rostral surfaces, with less distinct gradients on the medial surface. Gradients were generally least significant over the very center of the colliculus.

span.label: the electrode depth-penetration technique, reimplemented as cylinders driven normal to a modelled tissue surface so that fMRI voxels can be sampled along depth the way an electrode track samples laminae
span.quote: We use these cylinders to probe the variation of response difference (Figure 3 E) or centroid frequency (Figure 4 E) with depth in the tissue, a hemodynamic analog to making electrode penetrations into the tissue.

span.label: surface reconstruction and depth sampling, imported from cortex to a small subcortical nucleus
span.quote: The success of these surface-based analysis methods will enable more detailed non-invasive explorations of the functional architecture of other subcortical human auditory structures that have complex, laminar organization.

span.label: the electrode penetration itself, reimplemented as a virtual penetration through a hemodynamic volume
span.quote: Thus, the notion of using tissue depth as a reference frame was proven to work fairly well, despite the patchy character of the data.

span.label: tonotopy here is a DEPTH gradient measured along virtual penetrations normal to the tissue surface, not a gradient across a cortical sheet - the reference frame is the structure's own laminar geometry
span.quote: Thus, the notion of using tissue depth as a reference frame was proven to work fairly well, despite the patchy character of the data.

span.label: patchy versus continuous is the axis on which this result differs from the 4.7 T and 7 T studies, and the paper attributes the difference to what BOLD is sensitive to rather than to error
span.quote: The patchy nature of the topographical representation in our study may reflect the different neural sensitivity of BOLD fMRI. Specifically, various experiments indicate that fMRI is more sensitive to neuronal inputs (Logothetis et al., 2001 ), or to local-circuit activity (Angenstein et al., 2009 ). Accordingly, our results may more closely reflect the patchy, somewhat interdigitated tonotopic organization of bottom-up neuronal inputs to IC from the cochlear nucleus, as reported by anterograde labeling studies

span.label: the animal literature already contained both descriptions - electrophysiology finding fine continuous mapping, anterograde labelling finding patchy input - so patchy and smooth are both established before this study begins
span.quote: Similarly, anterograde labeling studies from the cochlear nucleus also show evidence for laminar frequency selectivity, but these results suggest a more heterogeneous, patchy distribution of frequency selectivity for the bottom-up inputs to IC

span.label: centroid frequency is the per-voxel preferred frequency, and its bootstrapped stability is reported before it is used
span.quote: The centroid frequency, f cent , was quite stable in all IC voxels. Bootstrapped confidence intervals had a mean value <0.5 octaves, and did not exceed 0.9 octaves. Thus, compared to the 5-octave frequency band of the stimuli, the experimental variability in centroid frequency was small, typically <

span.label: builds-on → Baumann et al. (2011)
span.quote: This procedure is analogous to that used by Baumann et al. ( 2011 ).

span.label: replicates → Schreiner and Langner (1997)
span.quote: Our results obtained from humans using non-invasive high (1.2 mm) resolution are largely consistent with invasive animal measurements of frequency preference in CN (Schreiner and Langner, 1997 ) as well as high-field neuroimaging studies, which indicate that individual neuronal frequency preferences are organized systematically by depth.

span.label: contradicts → Baumann et al. (2011) and De Martino et al. (2013)
span.quote: The patchy character of our results disagree with the much more continuous spatial gradient of tonotopic selectivity observed by Baumann et al. ( 2011 ) and De Martino et al. ( 2013 ).

span.label: confirms → invasive animal measurements of frequency preference organised systematically by depth in the central nucleus
span.quote: Our results obtained from humans using non-invasive high (1.2 mm) resolution are largely consistent with invasive animal measurements of frequency preference in CN (Schreiner and Langner, 1997 ) as well as high-field neuroimaging studies, which indicate that individual neuronal frequency preferences are organized systematically by depth.

span.label: contradicts → the continuous spatial gradient reported at 4.7 T in monkeys and 7 T in humans
span.quote: The patchy character of our results disagree with the much more continuous spatial gradient of tonotopic selectivity observed by Baumann et al. ( 2011 ) and De Martino et al. ( 2013 ).

span.label: supports → anterograde labelling studies reporting a patchy, interdigitated tonotopic input from cochlear nucleus
span.quote: The patchy nature of the topographical representation in our study may reflect the different neural sensitivity of BOLD fMRI. Specifically, various experiments indicate that fMRI is more sensitive to neuronal inputs (Logothetis et al., 2001 ), or to local-circuit activity (Angenstein et al., 2009 ). Accordingly, our results may more closely reflect the patchy, somewhat interdigitated tonotopic organization of bottom-up neuronal inputs to IC from the cochlear nucleus, as reported by anterograde labeling studies

span.label: qualifies → earlier midbrain fMRI, which could not resolve the internal topography at all
span.quote: While several studies have documented midbrain activity to auditory stimulation (Guimaraes et al., 1998 ; Hawley et al., 2005 ; Sigalovsky and Melcher, 2006 ; Rinne et al., 2007 ; Chandrasekaran et al., 2012 ), these studies could not determine the complex 3D functional topography of the IC because of their limited spatial resolution.

span.label: tonotopy —operationalised-as→ depth gradient
span.quote: Thus, the notion of using tissue depth as a reference frame was proven to work fairly well, despite the patchy character of the data.

span.label: RETRACTED (RE-GROUNDED) · central nucleus —distinct-from→ external cortex
span.quote: Since tonotopy is not a feature of the external cortex of the IC, this region is ignored in the subsequent depth analysis.

span.label: spatial smoothing —causes→ depth gradient
span.quote: We examined the effects of spatial smoothing on our data by blurring the original fMRI data volumes with a 2-mm FWHM Gaussian kernel, then repeating the same depth analysis (Figure S2 in Supplementary Material). Significant positive depth gradients are still evident, with spatial structure largely similar to that observed in the original data. However, the blurring tends to reduce the absolute magnitude of the depth gradients, and increases the area of reversed gradients observed at the margins of the colliculi.

span.label: BOLD —causes→ patchy
span.quote: The patchy nature of the topographical representation in our study may reflect the different neural sensitivity of BOLD fMRI. Specifically, various experiments indicate that fMRI is more sensitive to neuronal inputs (Logothetis et al., 2001 ), or to local-circuit activity (Angenstein et al., 2009 ). Accordingly, our results may more closely reflect the patchy, somewhat interdigitated tonotopic organization of bottom-up neuronal inputs to IC from the cochlear nucleus, as reported by anterograde labeling studies

span.label: RETRACTED (THE CONTAINMENT RUNS THE OTHER WAY) · inferior colliculus —part-of→ central nucleus
span.quote: Since tonotopy is not a feature of the external cortex of the IC, this region is ignored in the subsequent depth analysis.

span.label: central nucleus —distinct-from→ external cortex
span.quote: The IC consists of three prominent and functionally distinct subdivisions: the tonotopically organized central nucleus, the multisensory external cortex, and the dorsal cortex, which receives corticocollicular connections, primarily from the auditory cortex.

span.label: bootstrap
span.quote: Therefore, we used “bootstrapping,” a non-parametric method to estimate statistical significance.

span.label: confidence interval
span.quote: For our data here, we resampled the data with replacement 1000 times; error bars then show the 68% confidence intervals on the bootstrapped distribution, which is similar to what would be presented for the standard-error-of-the-mean for a normal distribution.

span.label: p-value
span.quote: The fraction of the resampled data sets with negative slopes provides an estimate of the p value for the gradient.

span.label: linear regression
span.quote: We then recorded the centroid frequency as a function of depth along the virtual penetration, and fit the result with a straight line; the slope of the fitted line, g , was an estimate of tonotopic gradient with depth.

span.label: weighted mean
span.quote: Specifically, we formed a weighted average: ⟨ n ⟩ = Σ i g i n i ∕ Σ i g i , where n i is the direction of each significant penetration i , having depth gradient g i .

span.label: bootstrapping instead of spatial blurring
span.quote: Typically, fMRI data is therefore “whitened” by performing a mixture of spatial and temporal blurring (Worsley and Friston, 1995 ; Friston et al., 2000 ). To maintain high spatial resolution, we wanted to avoid any blurring. Therefore, we used

span.label: linear fit of centroid frequency against depth
span.term: linear fit of centroid frequency against depth
span.quote: Mean gradient was 0.53 octaves/mm, about half of what would be required to linearly resolve the full stimulus gamut in a 5-mm depth of tissue (see Discussion ).

span.label: bootstrapped confidence intervals on centroid frequency
span.term: bootstrapped confidence intervals on centroid frequency
span.quote: The centroid frequency, f cent , was quite stable in all IC voxels. Bootstrapped confidence intervals had a mean value <0.5 octaves, and did not exceed 0.9 octaves. Thus, compared to the 5-octave frequency band of the stimuli, the experimental variability in centroid frequency was small, typically <

span.label: High-resolution 3 T fMRI resolves a depth tonotopy in human inferior colliculus, with superficial tissue preferring low frequencies and deeper tissue high frequencies, in both ICs of every subject.
span.quote: We observed significant tonotopy in the depth of IC tissue, with superficial layers showing greater preference to low frequencies and deeper layers to high frequencies.

span.label: Unlike the smooth gradients reported at 4.7 T and 7 T, the frequency map measured here is spatially patchy rather than continuous.
span.quote: In contrast to these studies, the detailed spatial structure of our preferred-frequency measurements shows a patchy character.

span.label: Re-running the whole analysis on data blurred with a 2-mm kernel reproduced the same patchy layout, so the patchiness is signal rather than thermal noise.
span.quote: This result indicates that the observed patchiness is a real feature of the data, and not the consequence of random noise.

span.label: Depth gradients were stronger and covered more tissue in the left colliculus than the right.
span.quote: Gradients were typically stronger and more extensive on the left colliculus then on the right.

span.label: Frequency tuning is broadest in the middle of the stimulus range: tuning widths at mid frequencies exceed those at the low and high ends by about 40%, giving an inverted-U profile.
span.quote: On average, tuning widths are about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies than they are at the lower and higher ends of the stimulus frequency band.

span.label: Paradoxically the very center of the colliculus, where a clean depth tonotopy was expected, showed the weakest gradients.
span.quote: In particular, we tend to observe weaker tonotopic depth gradients in the very center of the IC, an area expected to have a clearly organized depth tonotopy.

span.label: significant tonotopic depth gradients were found in both ICs of all four subjects
span.quote: Significant ( p < 0.05) patches of tonotopic representation with depth were evident in all subjects (Figure 5 ). Significant gradients varied from 0.3 to 1.2 octaves/mm.

span.label: superficial tissue prefers low frequencies and deeper tissue high frequencies
span.quote: Superficial voxels often displayed low-frequency preference, with a distinct low-pass response characteristic. Similarly, deep voxels often had high-pass characteristics. Voxels at intermediate depths had mid-frequency preferences overall, but had more heterogeneous response patterns that often included a mixture of low- and high-frequency response.

span.label: significant gradients covered only 18% of total bilateral IC area
span.quote: Areas of significant depth gradients varied from 19 to 32 mm 2 (mean across subjects of 25 mm 2 ), which was 18% of the total area of bilateral IC.

span.label: the mean gradient of 0.53 octaves/mm is about half what would span the stimulus range over 5 mm of tissue
span.quote: Mean gradient was 0.53 octaves/mm, about half of what would be required to linearly resolve the full stimulus gamut in a 5-mm depth of tissue (see Discussion ).

span.label: the organisation is patchy rather than continuous
span.quote: Much like the amplitude-difference data, the preferred-frequency responses exhibit patchy bands of frequency selectivity.

span.label: smoothing the data with a 2 mm kernel preserved the gradients but reduced their magnitude and increased spurious reversed gradients at the margins
span.quote: We examined the effects of spatial smoothing on our data by blurring the original fMRI data volumes with a 2-mm FWHM Gaussian kernel, then repeating the same depth analysis (Figure S2 in Supplementary Material). Significant positive depth gradients are still evident, with spatial structure largely similar to that observed in the original data. However, the blurring tends to reduce the absolute magnitude of the depth gradients, and increases the area of reversed gradients observed at the margins of the colliculi.

span.label: frequency tuning width follows an inverted-U, about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies
span.quote: On average, tuning widths are about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies than they are at the lower and higher ends of the stimulus frequency band. Bootstrapped reliability estimates indicate that tuning widths at both the lowest centroid frequencies (0.25–0.5 kHz) and highest centroid frequencies (4–8 kHz) are both significantly lower ( p < 0.02) than tuning widths at intermediate frequencies (1.5–3 kHz) for each individual subject.

span.label: the patchy structure is argued to be real rather than noise
span.quote: The observed structure is unlikely to be consequence of noise; they are a real feature of the data.

span.label: tonotopy
span.quote: Organization by frequency, tonotopy , is one of the central organizing principles of the auditory system.

span.label: sparse-sampling fMRI design
span.quote: In sparse-sampling designs, one attempts to sample the hyperoxic peak of the BOLD response evoked by preceding stimulus, then allocate a sufficient delay to allow that response to decay away before the next sample is obtained.

span.label: virtual penetration (cylindrical depth probe through IC tissue)
span.term: virtual penetration (cylindrical depth probe through IC tissue)
span.quote: We use these cylinders to probe the variation of response difference (Figure 3 E) or centroid frequency (Figure 4 E) with depth in the tissue, a hemodynamic analog to making electrode penetrations into the tissue.

span.label: the three subdivisions of the inferior colliculus
span.term: the three subdivisions of the inferior colliculus
span.quote: The IC consists of three prominent and functionally distinct subdivisions: the tonotopically organized central nucleus, the multisensory external cortex, and the dorsal cortex, which receives corticocollicular connections, primarily from the auditory cortex.

span.label: bootstrapping
span.quote: The bootstrapping procedure obtains a high-quality estimate of the statistical distribution of the observed data.

span.label: the depth-penetration reference frame
span.quote: Thus, the notion of using tissue depth as a reference frame was proven to work fairly well, despite the patchy character of the data.

span.label: sparse sampling
span.quote: In sparse-sampling designs, one attempts to sample the hyperoxic peak of the BOLD response evoked by preceding stimulus, then allocate a sufficient delay to allow that response to decay away before the next sample is obtained. Moreover, the delay is adjusted so that the nuisance response from the scanner-acquisition noise is minimized

span.label: center frequency of the bandpass-noise stimulus
span.term: center frequency of the bandpass-noise stimulus
span.quote: Auditory stimuli, presented through MRI compatible earphones, consisted of bandpass-filtered (0.6-octave bandwidth) white noise, presented with five different center frequencies, logarithmically spaced on 0.25–8 kHz (Figure 1 A).

span.label: depth into IC tissue along the virtual penetration
span.term: depth into IC tissue along the virtual penetration
span.quote: We then recorded the centroid frequency as a function of depth along the virtual penetration, and fit the result with a straight line; the slope of the fitted line, g , was an estimate of tonotopic gradient with depth.

span.label: BOLD response amplitude difference between highest and lowest stimulus frequency
span.term: BOLD response amplitude difference between highest and lowest stimulus frequency
span.quote: As a first form of analysis, we calculated the BOLD response amplitude differences between the highest and lowest stimulus frequencies (Figure 3 D).

span.label: attentional engagement, held constant by the concurrent discrimination task
span.term: attentional engagement, held constant by the concurrent discrimination task
span.quote: To ensure that participants paid consistent attention to the stimuli, they performed a challenging two-interval forced-choice frequency-discrimination task.

span.label: depth along the virtual penetration
span.quote: Thus, the notion of using tissue depth as a reference frame was proven to work fairly well, despite the patchy character of the data.

span.label: centroid frequency per voxel
span.quote: The centroid frequency, f cent , was quite stable in all IC voxels. Bootstrapped confidence intervals had a mean value <0.5 octaves, and did not exceed 0.9 octaves. Thus, compared to the 5-octave frequency band of the stimuli, the experimental variability in centroid frequency was small, typically <

span.label: tuning width
span.quote: The results show an “inverted-U” shape for all individual subjects, with a similar profile for all subjects taken together.

span.label: 0.3 to 1.2 octaves/mm — range of the statistically significant tonotopic depth gradients measured across subjects
span.quote: Significant gradients varied from 0.3 to 1.2 octaves/mm.

span.label: 0.53 octaves/mm — mean tonotopic depth gradient, about half the value needed to span the full stimulus range over 5 mm of tissue
span.quote: Mean gradient was 0.53 octaves/mm, about half of what would be required to linearly resolve the full stimulus gamut in a 5-mm depth of tissue (see Discussion ).

span.label: 18% — share of the total bilateral IC surface area carrying a significant depth gradient (19-32 mm2 per subject)
span.quote: Areas of significant depth gradients varied from 19 to 32 mm 2 (mean across subjects of 25 mm 2 ), which was 18% of the total area of bilateral IC.

span.label: 40% — how much broader frequency tuning is at intermediate frequencies than at the extremes of the stimulus band
span.quote: On average, tuning widths are about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies than they are at the lower and higher ends of the stimulus frequency band.

span.label: 75–85% — subjects' accuracy on the adaptive frequency-discrimination task across runs
span.quote: Across runs, subjects’ performance was 75–85% correct.

span.label: ∼20–30 — thermal SNR of the 1.2-mm images, against the >100 typical of conventional fMRI
span.quote: Conventional fMRI studies operate where the thermal SNR is typically >100; our images had SNR ∼20–30.

span.label: 1000 — number of bootstrap resamples used to derive the 68% confidence intervals
span.quote: For our data here, we resampled the data with replacement 1000 times; error bars then show the 68% confidence intervals on the bootstrapped distribution, which is similar to what would be presented for the standard-error-of-the-mean for a normal distribution.

span.label: four — number of subjects scanned
span.quote: Subjects were four male adults (age range 21–31), with normal hearing (air-conduction thresholds <20 dB nHL for octaves from 0.25 to 8 kHz).

span.label: 1.2 mm cubic voxels at 3 T — the resolution that made the measurement possible
span.quote: The goal of this study is to examine frequency representation in the human IC using high-resolution (1.2 mm) functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) at 3 T, adapted for auditory stimulation.

span.label: 0.3 to 1.2 octaves/mm, mean 0.53 — the measured depth gradients
span.quote: Significant ( p < 0.05) patches of tonotopic representation with depth were evident in all subjects (Figure 5 ). Significant gradients varied from 0.3 to 1.2 octaves/mm.

span.label: 18% of total bilateral IC area — how much of the structure showed a significant gradient
span.quote: Areas of significant depth gradients varied from 19 to 32 mm 2 (mean across subjects of 25 mm 2 ), which was 18% of the total area of bilateral IC.

span.label: R-squared about 0.5 — quality of the linear fit within each penetration
span.quote: Mean gradient was 0.53 octaves/mm, about half of what would be required to linearly resolve the full stimulus gamut in a 5-mm depth of tissue (see Discussion ).

span.label: IC under 9 mm — the size that made conventional imaging inadequate
span.quote: In humans, the small size of the IC (<9 mm), coupled with the limited resolution of conventional human neuroimaging studies, have precluded the non-invasive examination of frequency representation.

span.label: 3 to 10 mm sampling in conventional studies — the resolution at which the internal organisation is unresolvable
span.quote: Conventional functional neuroimaging studies employ 3–10 mm sampling and spatial blurring, making it impossible to resolve functional subdivisions within the IC.

span.label: about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies — the inverted-U in tuning width
span.quote: On average, tuning widths are about 40% broader at intermediate frequencies than they are at the lower and higher ends of the stimulus frequency band. Bootstrapped reliability estimates indicate that tuning widths at both the lowest centroid frequencies (0.25–0.5 kHz) and highest centroid frequencies (4–8 kHz) are both significantly lower ( p < 0.02) than tuning widths at intermediate frequencies (1.5–3 kHz) for each individual subject.
